evidence.section_title: THE ROLE OF PERFECTIONISM IN STUDENT SUICIDE: THREE CASE STUDIES FROM THE UK*

This article aims to provide important insight into the potency that certain profiles of perfectionism can claim in the path to suicide by presenting three case studies from a U.K. study of student suicide. Collectively, these case studies provide theoretical support for existing frameworks and are consistent with other literature which emphasizes those forms of perfectionism that engender severe self-criticism and self-doubt and fear of failure as most destructive.

[/page/1/Text/1] In all three cases clinical depression was identified, and a contributing element to suicidality, as traced out by the data, was perfectionism. [/page/1/Text/2] The article begins by outlining and comparing definitions of perfectionism and how it has been described in the suicide literature. We then outline a rationale for suggesting why some of the higher education student population may be particularly vulnerable to suicidal ideation and behavior. While perfectionism is unlikely to be the defining feature of an individual who takes their own life, these data about its possible importance are consistent with other psychological theories and research which draw attention to the destructive elements of the relationship between perfectionism and suicide. This article seeks to shed light upon the nature of this relationship and the influence perfectionism may have as a contributory factor to suicide.

[/page/5/Text/1] Initial analysis identified perfectionism (or similar constructs such as obsessive fear of failure, sensitivity to criticism, high self-criticism, etc.) as a factor which, from the perspective of those interviewed, contributed to the death to varying degrees from half (10) of the case studies.

[/page/5/Text/6] In this section we present data from three anonymized case studies (all described as gifted and talented students) which illustrate one of the main themes emerging from our study on student suicide; that of perfectionism. [/page/6/Text/2] (and acknowledging its similarity to maladaptive and clinical perfectionism), develops and interprets this theme according to three theoretical frameworks: Blatt's (1995) account of the destructiveness of perfectionism, Burns's (1980) analysis of the perfectionist's script for self-defeat, and Pacht's (1984) reflections on perfection.

Ryan was described as an extremely high achiever in all aspects. However, these accounts reveal that Ryan suffered acute anxiety around his academic performance, personal achievement, and appearance, which manifested itself in a number of physical and psychological symptoms. His parents explained how the onset of his problems began when he started studying hard for examinations around the age of 16 (called exams in the extract below). They could see the effect it was having on him, because there were occasions when he became emotional and would break down and cry due to the strain he placed on himself:

his parents recall the onset of depression at around the age of 14. They remember noticeable mood swings at that point (used to be high—energetic and creative—and he used to be low). ... he lost all confidence when he went to university. It seems university life didn't match up to his expectations and he became disillusioned. During this time, he experienced intense doubts about his ability to succeed in his course, severe doubts about his ability to hold a relationship together, and suffered disappointments of different kinds (where he over-reacted to making mistakes). ... his parents identified his dissatisfaction with academic progress as a major point of frustration: ... Sam's perception that the breakdown of two relationships meant he was a social failure is indicative of the dichotomous (all or nothing) thinking common among perfectionists. ... This, in turn, triggered periods of anxiety and depression; it turned the high hopes and expectations he had for himself and others to disillusionment, frustration, and despair. ... He said he felt depressed. Letters written by him shortly before his death reveal he was consumed with self-doubt, and had become highly self-critical and disillusioned...

Dan was described by his father, and others who knew him before he went to university, as a high achiever. ... He became much more "closed" and "introverted." His academic progress was irregular and at the end of his first year he failed two of his exams. Suffering from depression he re-sat these exams but failed again. ... The first early indication of Dan's perfectionistic thinking was hinted at by one of his friends... his own high expectations and heightened self-criticism distinguished him from his friends. ... diagnosed him as suffering from depression (with suicidal ideation)... it revolves really around being very critical of himself, never thinking it would come to this kind of thing. ... one of his friends attributed the onset of Dan's depression to academic over-striving and his intense need to avoid failure. ... the role that Dan's sensitivity toward failure played in his suicide. ... just feel like a failure. ... his worst thing was failure, he hated failure, and I suppose failing his first year at Uni was obviously a massive trigger. ... The letter he left said he felt like a black cloud hanging over his family and friends. ... In the event of failure his self-criticism and perfectionism seemed to predispose him to levels of depression (and the potential for suicide). Dan's suicide note conveyed a sense of profound personal failure; a feeling that he had let everyone down and a belief that he had failed to meet the expectations of the people who mattered most.

The type of stress Ryan was reported as suffering was suggested by Burns (1980) and Pacht (1984) to be symptomatic of neurotic perfectionism (Hamacheck, 1978) where individuals are driven by relentless standards to the point of agony. An inability to enjoy the fruits of his accomplishment, according to Hamacheck (1978), is also characteristic of neurotic or maladaptive perfectionism and seemed to be shared experiences among the case studies. Not only is perfection an undesirable goal, from this point of view, it is a debilitating one as well. The drive for perfection maintains people in psychological turmoil precisely because that perfection is nonexistent. An intense need to avoid failure was argued by Blatt (1995) to force the neurotically perfectionistic individual into an endless cycle of self-defeating over-striving in which each task becomes another threatening challenge, as seemed to be happening to Dan in particular. Blatt (1995) also argued that the inability to enjoy accomplishments is characteristic of neurotic perfectionism and can result in increased susceptibility to depression and suicide. Burns (1980) argued that when students (with entrenched perfectionistic thinking patterns) begin to realize that their performance will place them somewhere in the middle of the pack, they react with frustration, anger, depression, and panic. This seemed applicable to the case of Sam. Burns (1980) further suggested that as the gap between expectation and actual performance widens, students begin to experience stress and an aversion to learning. This may also be accompanied by painful mood swings and loss of self-esteem, which happened for Sam. The portrait of Sam that emerged from his ex-girlfriend is consistent with Burns' (1980) characterization of perfectionistic individuals as "compulsives" who are especially given to troubled relationships and mood disorders. This type of cognitive distortion, according to Burns (1980), brings fear of mistakes and overreaction. It also leads to overgeneralizations (systems of cognitive distortion common among perfectionists), where they jump to the conclusion that a negative event will be repeated endlessly and predict negative future outcomes (hence his perception that he had a social problem and also his fear of appearing foolish or inadequate among his peers). Blatt (1995) accounts for the destructiveness of this type of personality style by arguing that intense perfectionism can result in a marked vulnerability to experiences of failure and criticism, and an increased susceptibility to ensuing depression and suicide, as seemed to be happening to the young men described here. Because their previous experiences have left them psychologically unprepared for an "average" role, they are prone to perceive themselves, unrealistically, as second rate losers. Their self-respect plummets, and they experience a strong desire to withdraw from painful circumstances. The disturbance can become so intense that they may contemplate and even attempt suicide.

Collectively, our case studies support the work of Burns (1980), Pacht (1984), and Blatt (1995) and are consistent with other literature which emphasizes the complex and most destructive elements of the relationship between perfectionism and suicide. In the first of our case studies, Ryan's striving for perfection drove him to the point of agony and eventually despair. In the second, Sam's self-criticism and self-doubt, together with unrealistically ideal expectations and dichotomous thinking, made for a devastating combination. For Dan, who was also highly self-critical and terrified of failure, the reality of failure was finally too much to bear. Perfectionism predisposed all three of these individuals to anxiety and depression. In all three we catch sight of the psychological turmoil affected by a uniquely untenable position: the setting of exceptionally high standards and hopes but with no room for alternatives presents a no-win scenario because that perfection is nonexistent. People with such high personal standards and perfectionistic expectations are therefore likely to experience more punishment than reward in life (Burns, 1980) and are likely to end up frustrated. Thus, there is nothing wrong with having high standards and expectations, but when perfectionistic thinking is accompanied by excessive self-criticism and self-doubt, obsessive fear of failure, the inability to enjoy achievements, and the type of "all or nothing" thinking where anything other than complete success is perceived to be equivalent to total failure, the components for potential catastrophe may be at hand. While explanations for suicides are always complex, and for some cases the relative contribution of perfectionism will vary, this article has focused on the extreme potency that certain profiles of perfectionism can claim in the path to suicide. Our analyses provide important insights into the efficacy of existing theories and the destructive forces that lead some talented but exceptionally self-critical and perfectionistic young people to take their own lives.
